question: How does self-attention work in the Transformer?
answer:
Self‑attention computes three vectors—queries (Q), keys (K) and values (V)—by linearly projecting the same input sequence (the output of the previous layer).  The attention scores are obtained with scaled dot‑product similarity between each query and all keys, followed by a softmax that weights the corresponding values, so every position can attend to every other position in the same layer [attention_is_all_you_need_v7.pdf, p. 5].

The Transformer uses **multi‑head** self‑attention: the projected Q, K, V are split into h parallel heads, each performing the attention operation independently (with dimensions dk = dv = dmodel/h).  The resulting head outputs are concatenated and linearly transformed to produce the final attention output, allowing the model to capture information from different representation subspaces simultaneously [attention_is_all_you_need_v7.pdf, p. 5].

In the encoder, all Q, K and V come from the encoder’s own previous layer, so each token can attend to every other token in the input sequence.  In the decoder, self‑attention also uses the decoder’s own previous layer but masks out future positions (by setting their softmax inputs to −∞) to preserve the auto‑regressive property [attention_is_all_you_need_v7.pdf, p. 5].

question: What is the purpose of multi-head attention?
answer: Multi‑head attention is introduced so that a model can attend simultaneously to information coming from different representation subspaces and at different positions, rather than collapsing everything into a single averaged view. question: How does masking work in the Transformer decoder?
answer:
In the decoder’s self‑attention layer a mask is applied so that each position can only attend to earlier positions in the output sequence. The mask blocks attention scores for any “future” token (i.e., positions > i) and thus prevents the model from using information that has not yet been generated [attention_is_all_you_need_v7.pdf, p. 3].

Because the output embeddings are shifted by one position, this masked self‑attention guarantees that the prediction for position i can depend solely on the already‑produced tokens at positions < i, enforcing an autoregressive decoding process [attention_is_all_you_need_v7.pdf, p. 3].

question: How are queries, keys, and values used in scaled dot-product attention?
answer:
In scaled dot‑product attention each query vector is compared with every key vector by taking their dot product; the resulting scores are divided by √dₖ to temper their magnitude and then passed through a softmax to produce a set of attention weights [attention_is_all_you_need_v7.pdf, p. 4].

question: How does Moshi support real-time speech interaction?
answer:
Moshi enables real‑time spoken dialogue by treating conversation as speech‑to‑speech generation rather than a cascade of separate modules.  It runs a multi‑stream Transformer that models the system’s speech and the user’s speech in parallel token streams, removing the need for explicit speaker‑turn segmentation and allowing overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections to be handled continuously.  This full‑duplex design yields a theoretical latency of 160 ms and about 200 ms in practice, making interaction comparable to a natural conversation【moshi_v1.pdf, p. 1】.  

The model generates tokens hierarchically in a streaming fashion: a text language‑model backbone (Helium) first predicts time‑aligned text tokens (“Inner Monologue”), which are then used as a prefix for semantic and acoustic tokens produced by a residual‑vector‑quantized neural audio codec (Mimi).  This simultaneous production of text, semantic and acoustic tokens provides streaming speech recognition and text‑to‑speech, while also allowing the synthesis of varied emotions, voices and acoustic conditions in real time【moshi_v1.pdf, p. 6】.

question: How does Moshi combine speech and text generation?
answer:
Moshi merges speech and text generation through its **Inner Monologue** architecture, which breaks a speech utterance into a structured chain of three token types: text tokens, semantic audio tokens, and acoustic audio tokens. The model predicts this hierarchy in a single Transformer, so the same generative network can output both the textual transcription and the corresponding speech representation without needing separate models [moshi_v1.pdf, p. 5].

The hierarchical prediction is performed **per‑frame**, meaning each generation step produces a speech frame rather than waiting for an entire text sequence to be completed. This contrasts with earlier “Chain‑of‑Modality” approaches (e.g., Spectron) that first generate a full text prefix before producing audio tokens, and it enables Moshi to operate in real time for streaming TTS and ASR [moshi_v1.pdf, p. 5].

By keeping text and speech tokens within the same sequence, Inner Monologue allows any utterance to be represented simultaneously as text and as speech, supporting arbitrary voice conditions and avoiding an increase in Transformer output length. The design therefore provides a unified, real‑time speech‑text foundation model for dialogue [moshi_v1.pdf, p. 5].

question: What is dynamic chunking in hierarchical sequence modeling?
answer:
Dynamic chunking is a learned, data‑dependent subsampling mechanism that compresses input sequences in a content‑aware way by optimizing the chunk boundaries end‑to‑end together with the rest of the model [dynamic_chunking_v2.pdf, p. 4].  

In hierarchical sequence modeling, this mechanism enables the network to build higher‑level abstractions from low‑level data—effectively “chunking” tokens into larger semantic units—so that each hierarchical stage processes a progressively compressed representation, improving compute efficiency and reasoning over the sequence [dynamic_chunking_v2.pdf, p. 4].

question: Why is chunking used in hierarchical sequence modeling?
answer:
Chunking groups low‑level tokens into higher‑level units, turning raw data into abstract representations that can be processed more efficiently — it reduces the sequence length while preserving semantic structure, enabling the model to reason over compressed inputs with fewer compute and parameters [dynamic_chunking_v2.pdf, p. 4].

Hierarchical models exploit this by first using small byte‑level networks to compress the raw stream into subsampled sequences and then applying a stronger language model to the resulting chunks, which improves overall efficiency compared with naïve pooling or token‑based approaches [dynamic_chunking_v2.pdf, p. 2].

Because the learned chunks correspond to semantically coherent units, the approach also yields greater robustness to perturbations and better interpretability, especially for languages lacking clear segmentation cues [dynamic_chunking_v2.pdf, p. 4].

question: How does dynamic chunking differ from fixed-size chunking?
answer:

In contrast, fixed‑size (static) chunking applies uniform, predetermined windows that ignore natural semantic boundaries, often cutting words or phrases arbitrarily and limiting model expressivity [dynamic_chunking_v2.pdf, p. 32].
